(CNN) -- The mother and brother of a 31-year-old woman found strangled with her two young sons in the bedrooms of their home filed a wrongful death lawsuit Tuesday against the alleged killer -- the husband and father of the victims. Christopher Coleman has pleaded not guilty and is being held without bond. Christopher Coleman has pleaded not guilty in the triple homicide police say took place early in the morning on May 5 in the family home in the small southwestern Illinois city of Columbia. "To strip the culpable party of all financial holdings -- all that he has now and all that he may ever have," is the aim of the suit, said a statement accompanying the suit filed in Monroe County circuit court by Angela DeCicco and Mario Weiss, the mother and brother of Sheri Coleman. "To allow one penny of ill-gotten gain to be derived at the expense of Sheri, Garett and Gavin is not acceptable to those who dearly love them." The money would go to a memorial fund set up for Coleman and her sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9 and "these funds will be used to erect a lasting tribute in the city of Columbia," according to the complaint. "Our goal is to extract something positive from such a horrific and senseless tragedy and to honor the lives of my sister and her two young sons," Weiss said. The wrongful death suit also names Coleman's father, Ronald, and the Joyce Meyer Ministries, where Coleman worked until shortly after his family was killed, as "respondents in discovery," which means they may be forced to hand over financial documents and information such as Coleman's personnel file, his work schedule and travel itineraries and the Ministries' employment policies. In addition, the suit tries to establish a timeline of events before and after the killings, saying the Colemans took the deed to their home in 2005, but six months ago, ownership was transferred to Christoper Coleman alone. "Sheri did not voluntarily sign the deed transferring title to the residence to Christopher," the document says. Lawyers in the civil suit also allege that in the period between the killings and his arrest, Coleman removed personal property from the home. The suit asks that Coleman and anyone "acting at his direction" be forbidden from entering the home again and that he provide a list of items already removed. Coleman remains in jail after a judge denied bond.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- The mother and brother of a 31-year-old woman who was found strangled alongside her two young sons in the bedrooms of their home filed a wrongful death lawsuit Tuesday against the alleged killer—the victims’ husband and father.

Christopher Coleman has pleaded not guilty to the triple homicide, which police say occurred early on the morning of May 5 at the family’s home in Columbia, a small city in southwestern Illinois. He is being held without bond.

“The aim of the suit is to strip the culpable party of all financial holdings—all that he has now and all that he may ever have,” said a statement accompanying the lawsuit, filed in Monroe County Circuit Court by Angela DeCicco and Mario Weiss, the mother and brother of Sheri Coleman.

“To allow one penny of ill-gotten gain to be derived at the expense of Sheri, Garett and Gavin is not acceptable to those who dearly love them.”

According to the complaint, any money recovered would go to a memorial fund established for Coleman and her sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9. “These funds will be used to erect a lasting tribute in the city of Columbia,” the complaint states.

“Our goal is to extract something positive from such a horrific and senseless tragedy and to honor the lives of my sister and her two young sons,” Weiss said.

The wrongful death lawsuit also names Coleman’s father, Ronald, and Joyce Meyer Ministries—where Coleman worked until shortly after his family was killed—as “respondents in discovery.” That designation means they may be compelled to provide financial records and other information, including Coleman’s personnel file, work schedule and travel itineraries, as well as the ministry’s employment policies.

The lawsuit also seeks to establish a timeline of events before and after the killings. It states that the Colemans obtained the deed to their home in 2005 but that, six months ago, ownership was transferred solely to Christopher Coleman.

“Sheri did not voluntarily sign the deed transferring title to the residence to Christopher,” the document states.

Attorneys in the civil case also allege that Coleman removed personal property from the home between the killings and his arrest. The lawsuit asks that Coleman and anyone “acting at his direction” be barred from entering the home again and that he provide a list of the items already removed.

Coleman remains in jail after a judge denied bond.

(CNN) — Angela DeCicco and Mario Weiss, the mother and brother of Sheri Coleman, filed a wrongful death lawsuit Tuesday against Christopher Coleman, Sheri’s husband and the father of her children, accusing him of killing the family.

Sheri Coleman, 31, and her sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9, were found strangled in bedrooms inside their home in Columbia, a small city in southwestern Illinois. Police say the three were killed early on May 5.

Christopher Coleman has entered a not-guilty plea to the three homicide charges. He remains jailed without bond after a judge refused to grant his release.

The lawsuit, filed in Monroe County Circuit Court, seeks to take from Coleman “all that he has now and all that he may ever have,” according to a statement submitted with the complaint.

Sheri Coleman’s relatives said they would not accept Coleman receiving “one penny of ill-gotten gain” at the expense of Sheri, Garett and Gavin.

Any money recovered would be placed in a memorial fund established in their names. The complaint says the money would finance a permanent tribute in Columbia.

Weiss said the family hopes to create something positive from the “horrific and senseless tragedy” while honoring his sister and her two young sons.

The civil action also lists Coleman’s father, Ronald, and Joyce Meyer Ministries—Coleman’s employer until shortly after the deaths—as “respondents in discovery.” That designation could require them to provide financial records and other material, including Coleman’s personnel file, work schedule and travel plans, as well as the ministry’s employment policies.

The lawsuit also attempts to determine the sequence of events surrounding the killings. It states that the Colemans received the deed to their home in 2005, but that ownership was transferred solely to Christopher Coleman six months ago. According to the filing, Sheri did not willingly sign the document transferring the property to her husband.

Attorneys in the civil case further claim that Coleman took personal belongings from the residence between the killings and his arrest. They are asking the court to bar both Coleman and anyone acting under his instructions from re-entering the house and to require him to identify everything already removed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about the wrongful death lawsuit filed by Sheri Coleman’s mother and brother against Christopher Coleman following the murders of Sheri and her two sons in Columbia, Illinois.
counterfactuals.output:
**Family files wrongful death lawsuit against convicted Illinois killer**

**COLUMBIA, Illinois —** The mother and brother of Sheri Coleman have filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Christopher Coleman, who was convicted of killing Sheri and the couple’s two young sons inside their Columbia, Illinois, home.

The civil complaint seeks damages arising from the May 2009 deaths of Sheri Coleman, 31, and her sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9. All three were found strangled in their beds.

Prosecutors said Christopher Coleman killed his family while pursuing an extramarital relationship and hoping to avoid a divorce that could threaten his job. Coleman had worked in security for Joyce Meyer Ministries.

Before the killings, Coleman reported receiving threatening messages that appeared to target his family because of his employment. Investigators later concluded he had sent the threats himself in an effort to create a false explanation for the murders.

A jury found Coleman guilty of three counts of first-degree murder in 2011. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

The wrongful death action is separate from the criminal case. It seeks to hold Coleman financially responsible for the losses suffered by Sheri Coleman’s surviving relatives and her estate. A civil lawsuit requires a lower burden of proof than a criminal prosecution, although Coleman’s convictions already established his criminal responsibility for the deaths.

Coleman maintained his innocence during the criminal proceedings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the latest legal developments in the Christopher Coleman triple-homicide case, including the civil suit, the memorial fund, property-transfer allegations, and the involvement of Joyce Meyer Ministries.
counterfactuals.output:
Christopher Coleman’s criminal case is effectively settled: he remains convicted of the 2009 strangulation murders of his wife, Sheri, and their sons, Garett and Gavin, and is serving three consecutive life sentences without parole. The later litigation has focused primarily on money, assets, and potential third-party liability.

- **Wrongful-death/civil litigation:** Representatives of Sheri and the children’s estates pursued claims against Coleman and sought to reach assets allegedly moved beyond the estates’ reach. Coleman’s civil liability was separate from his criminal conviction; the major contested issue was whether other people or entities could also be held responsible.

- **Joyce Meyer Ministries:** The estates argued that the ministry—where Coleman was security chief—knew of his affair, knew the affair could cost him his job, and failed to respond appropriately despite the threats directed at his family. The ministry denied responsibility, emphasizing that the killings were private criminal acts outside Coleman’s employment. Courts rejected the effort to impose wrongful-death liability on the ministry, finding that knowledge of an affair or employment-policy violation did not make a triple murder reasonably foreseeable and did not create a legal duty to protect Coleman’s family from him.

- **Memorial fund:** The civil pleadings also questioned the handling of money collected in memory of Sheri, Garett, and Gavin. The estates alleged that funds solicited for memorial or family-related purposes were placed under the control of, or transferred to, Coleman’s parents and were not preserved for the victims’ estates as donors would have expected. Those assertions were framed as accounting, conversion, or improper-transfer issues—not as proof that the ministry participated in the murders. Joyce Meyer Ministries disputed wrongdoing in connection with the fund.

- **Property-transfer allegations:** The estates alleged that, after the killings and while Coleman faced prosecution, valuable property—including his interest in the family home and other assets—was transferred to his parents or otherwise rearranged to keep it from potential wrongful-death creditors. The civil plaintiffs sought to set aside those transactions as fraudulent transfers and to trace proceeds from any later sale or disposition. Coleman’s parents were drawn into the litigation because they allegedly received or controlled the transferred property, although those allegations did not amount to accusations that they were involved in the homicides.

In short, the conviction and life sentences remain intact. The significant post-trial legal developments concerned whether the victims’ estates could recover from transferred assets, the memorial fund, Coleman’s parents, or Joyce Meyer Ministries. The attempt to hold the ministry liable for failing to prevent the murders was unsuccessful; the asset and fund disputes were narrower civil matters focused on ownership, accounting, and collectability.

Sheri Coleman’s family filed a wrongful-death complaint against her husband, Christopher Coleman, after Sheri, 31, and the couple’s sons, Garett, 11, and Gavin, 9, were found strangled in their Columbia, Illinois, home on May 5, 2009.

The civil action alleged that Coleman killed all three and sought damages for their deaths, as well as to prevent him from benefiting financially from their estates or insurance proceeds. Relatives said the case was “not about the money,” but about obtaining “justice for Sheri, Garett and Gavin.” Sheri’s mother said she wanted Coleman held accountable, adding, “He took everything from me.”

The complaint’s accusations paralleled the state’s criminal case. Prosecutors charged Coleman with three counts of first-degree murder, alleging that he strangled his wife and sons and then staged the home to make the killings appear connected to threatening messages he had reported receiving. Investigators said the threats and spray-painted writings were part of an effort to divert suspicion. Prosecutors also presented the theory that Coleman wanted to leave his marriage and continue a relationship with another woman.

Coleman pleaded not guilty. At the time of the civil filing, he remained in the Monroe County Jail, unable to post the $5 million bond set in his criminal case. The wrongful-death allegations were civil claims and did not constitute a criminal finding of guilt. Coleman was later convicted on all three murder counts and sentenced to life in prison without parole.

**COLUMBIA, Ill. —** Relatives of Sheri Coleman and her two sons have filed a civil lawsuit aimed at preventing her husband, Christopher Coleman, from profiting from their deaths.

Coleman is accused of strangling Sheri and their sons, Garett and Gavin, inside the family’s Columbia home. He has pleaded not guilty, and the criminal charges remain pending.

The civil action seeks to preserve the family’s assets and block Coleman from benefiting through the estate, the sale of the house or any other proceeds connected to the killings. It also raises questions about a deed that purportedly transferred an interest in the home to Coleman’s parents. The plaintiffs dispute that transaction and are asking the court to determine who legally owns the property.

The family has proposed demolishing the house and creating a memorial at the site for Sheri, Garett and Gavin. Any such plan would depend on the outcome of the property dispute and local approval.

The filing names Christopher Coleman as a defendant and lists his parents, Ronald and Connie Coleman, as respondents in discovery. Under Illinois law, that designation allows plaintiffs to seek information from people who may have relevant evidence and, if warranted, later ask that they be added as defendants.

No court has yet resolved the deed dispute or the civil claims. Coleman is presumed innocent in the criminal case unless and until he is found guilty.
